summary: Sixth-order light on a stone pier in the channel opposite Bristol Ferry, lit 1873; the 1938 hurricane led to its demolition and an automatic skeletal-tower light.

structures.note: Hexagonal tower attached to the keeper's house (D'Entremont). Archive: 19 feet from base to lantern, red daymark, light 33 feet above water. Demolished in 1939 after hurricane damage (Archive).
Automatic light on a skeletal tower (Archive; D'Entremont).

access.note: The U.S. Lighthouse Society Digital Archive lists the light as not open to the public.

events.note: Lighthouse Board recommended a light and fog bell (D'Entremont).
Light established 1 August 1873 after a $3,000 appropriation in March 1873 (D'Entremont); Archive gives year established 1873.
Hexagonal tower attached to the keeper's house (D'Entremont); Archive gives tower established 1873.
Sixth-order Fresnel lens (Archive: year original lens installed 1873).
Winter 1874 to 1875 ice floes moved the entire station four feet (D'Entremont).
$6,000 obtained March 1877; stone pier enlarged; lighthouse and dwelling rebuilt; fog bell mounted on the roof with a short tower and lantern (D'Entremont).
Keeper William Tengren and his son rescued two women and a man from an overturned power boat, 20 July (Bulletin).
Early February 1920 ice dislodged riprap and a large foundation stone (Bulletin); D'Entremont says the structure was soon rebuilt.
Keeper P. J. Brides picked up a man who had jumped or fallen overboard near the steamer Plymouth, 28 April. The Bulletin gives the station's state as New York; see notes_for_editor.
Ceiling of the four-room dwelling caved in, summer 1938 (D'Entremont).
Devastated by the hurricane of 21 September 1938 (D'Entremont); Archive disposition: 'Demolished in 1939 After Hurricane Damage'.
Building dismantled (D'Entremont); Archive: demolished in 1939 after hurricane damage.
Automatic light on a skeletal tower installed (Archive: 'Replaced with Skeletal Tower W/fixed Acetylene Light'; D'Entremont).

corrections.why: The 1873 wooden tower was demolished in 1939 after hurricane damage (Archive disposition; D'Entremont). The structure standing on the site today is the 1939 skeletal-tower light, not the 1873 tower the record lists as standing.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The record gives 1938 (Rowlett; Wikidata). The Archive gives the year discontinued as 1939, and says demolished in 1939 after hurricane damage; D'Entremont says the building was dismantled the following year after the 1938 storm. 1939 is used.

The Archive gives 33 feet above water (10 m) and D'Entremont 31 feet above sea level (about 9.4 m), both for the 1873 light. The record's 7.9 m (26 ft) has no cited source here, so no focal height is set for the current light.
The record's 1939 built and first_lit events are for the skeletal-tower light. The first light is 1873 (Archive; D'Entremont).
A structure is mapped on the site today; it is the 1939 skeletal-tower light. The 1873 tower is lost.

The Archive roster and D'Entremont differ on early dates and spellings: Dunwell (1873-1875 vs Dunnell 1874-1875), Smith (1875 vs 1876), Jansen (Evard vs Edward, 1908). The roster spelling and dates are used; the variants are in the keeper notes.

notes_for_editor: 1) The 1871 recommendation, the March 1873 appropriation ($3,000), the 1 August 1873 lighting, the 1874-75 ice, the March 1877 appropriation ($6,000), and the 31-foot height all come from D'Entremont alone. The Lighthouse Board volumes for 1871 to 1880 are not in the local corpus; two newspaper searches (Musselbed, 1873-74) found nothing. 2) The 1935 Bulletin names 'P. J. Brides, keeper of Musselbed Light Station, N. Y.' The Archive has Patrick J. Brides at Mussel Bed Shoals, Rhode Island, 1924-1939, and no other Musselbed light appears in the sources read. The Bulletin's state is either wrong or the report concerns another station; the story now says the rescue is not confirmed for this station. 3) Wikipedia (leads only, not cited) gives: a square house with integral tower, deactivated 1938, focal height 8 m, first lit August 1873, and says the first lighthouse was rebuilt in 1924. The rebuild date is not confirmed by a primary source here; D'Entremont says 'soon rebuilt' after the 1919-20 ice. 4) The Bulletins 1936 to 1939 contain no mention of Mussel Bed Shoals by name in the text read, so the 1938 storm damage here rests on D'Entremont and the Archive. 5) The 1913 rescue line is OCR'd ('Mussel Bed Shoa,]'); matched by context, and the 1912 to 1917 index (p. 48) supports the same keeper. 6) The Archive roster has William Tengren here 1909 to 1916 and at Bullock's Point 1901 to 1909 and 1916 to 1926; D'Entremont's Bullock's page agrees. 7) The Lime Rock Light station has no station id in the data set; the other_stations entry for Evard Jansen carries no id. 8) Printed page numbers of the 1894 Light-House Board volume are not confirmed; scan page 376 is given. 9) The Archive's coordinates (41 38.11 N, 71 15.38 W) and the record's coordinates differ by about 0.3 km; not corrected here. 10) The USCG Historian's page could not be read through the Internet Archive, so no USCG history is used. 11) The current light's characteristic is set to Fl R 6s from the record and D'Entremont (flashing red every six seconds); the original 1873 light was fixed red (D'Entremont).
